---
title: "Population 1: Standard Normal"
format:
  html:
    embed-resources: true
    toc: true
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
source("R/clt_functions.R")
student_id <- 5405
```

## 1. What population am I sampling from?

The population is the standard normal distribution, N(0, 1), with mean μ = 0 and standard deviation σ = 1. It is continuous, symmetric, and bell-shaped, with skewness 0 and excess kurtosis 0. The histogram of 10,000 individual values above shows this shape. This population serves as my control experiment: since it is already normal, any reasonable normality rule should classify its sample means as normal at every sample size. If my rule failed here, the rule itself would be flawed.

```{r}
#| label: population
set.seed(student_id)
pop <- rnorm(10000)
hist(pop, breaks = 40, main = "Population: Standard Normal",
     xlab = "Individual value")
```

## 2. What did I expect?

I expected the sampling distribution of the mean to be approximately normal at every sample size, including n = 1. The average of independent normal values is itself exactly normal, so the CLT isn’t needed here. At n = 1, each “sample mean” is just a single observation, so the sampling distribution is identical to the population. I expected skewness and kurtosis near 0 and a Q-Q correlation very close to 1 for every n, with only small differences due to Monte Carlo noise.

## 3. Which sample sizes did I investigate?

```{r}
#| label: sweep
set.seed(student_id)
results <- sweep_n(function(n) rnorm(n), n_values = c(1, 2, 5, 10, 30))
results
```

I tested n = 1, 2, 5, 10, and 30, each with B = 10,000 Monte Carlo repetitions. I started at n = 1, the smallest possible sample size, to check whether normality holds from the very beginning. I included n = 30 because it is the common rule of thumb. Since every value passed, there was no cutoff to narrow in on, so a finer grid was unnecessary.

## 4. When did it become approximately normal?

n = 1
The sampling distribution of the mean is approximately normal at every sample size tested, starting at n = 1.

## 5. Why did I choose that value?

```{r}
#| label: plots-n1
set.seed(student_id)
means_n1 <- simulate_means(function(n) rnorm(n), n = 1)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(means_n1, breaks = 40, probability = TRUE,
     main = "Sample means, n = 1", xlab = "Sample mean")
curve(dnorm(x, 0, 1), add = TRUE, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
qqnorm(means_n1, main = "Q-Q plot, n = 1")
qqline(means_n1, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

My rule calls a distribution approximately normal when |skewness| < 0.2, |excess kurtosis| < 0.5, and the Q-Q correlation is above 0.998, with no visible problems in the histogram or Q-Q plot.

All five sample sizes passed every check. The largest skewness was 0.029 and the largest excess kurtosis in absolute value was 0.082, both far inside my limits. The Q-Q correlation was 0.9999 at every n. These small nonzero values are consistent with Monte Carlo noise at B = 10,000 (about ±0.025 for skewness and ±0.05 for kurtosis), not real departures from normality.

The graphs agree. At n = 1, the histogram closely follows the N(0, 1) density curve, and the Q-Q plot falls along the reference line from end to end, with no curvature or peeling tails. Because the smallest possible sample size already passes, n = 1 is the answer.

## 6. What surprised me?

I expected skewness and kurtosis to shrink steadily toward 0 as n increased, but they didn’t. For example, excess kurtosis was 0.000 at n = 1 but −0.082 at n = 30, slightly further from 0. This happens because the sampling distribution is exactly normal at every n, so there is nothing to improve. The differences between rows are just random Monte Carlo noise. This showed me that, with simulated data, small changes in a statistic should not be over-interpreted; I need to compare them with the expected noise level before drawing conclusions.
